tx.t: This lecture looks at the history and the future of electric cars. Electric vehicles are older than many people think. The first ones appeared in the eighteen thirties.
Around the year nineteen hundred, more than a quarter of the cars on American roads were electric. Petrol cars then became cheaper and could travel further, so electric cars almost disappeared.

Modern electric cars use lithium-ion batteries, which store more energy for their weight. Their main advantage is that they produce no exhaust gases while driving, though making the batteries does cause pollution.

tx.t: Today we look at how printing changed the world. Before printing, every book in Europe was copied by hand, usually by monks, which took months.
Around fourteen forty, a German goldsmith called Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press with movable metal letters. The famous Gutenberg Bible was printed around fourteen fifty-five.
William Caxton set up the first printing press in England in fourteen seventy-six. Cheaper books helped literacy spread and made it easier to share new scientific ideas.

tx.t: This lecture is about a successful conservation project in the Calder Estuary. In nineteen eighty-five, only thirty-nine pairs of bats were counted there.
The main reason for the decline was disturbance from walkers and dogs. So volunteers and rangers created protected zones with quiet paths.
By twenty eleven, the number had risen to two hundred and forty-two pairs, which shows that careful management can work.

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the history of the Olympic Games. The ancient Games began in seven hundred and seventy-six BC at Olympia in Greece.

They were held every four years for about twelve centuries, until they were banned in the late fourth century. The modern Games were revived in eighteen ninety-six in Athens, mainly through the efforts of a Frenchman, Pierre de Coubertin.
Women first took part in the Games in nineteen hundred, in Paris. The first Winter Games were held in nineteen twenty-four at Chamonix, in France.
Today, thousands of athletes from more than two hundred countries compete in the summer Games.

In eighteen forty-eight, the population was about four thousand. Over the next fifty years it grew to thirty-seven thousand.
Then things changed, because the railway came and brought cheaper goods from the cities. As a result, many small traders went out of business.

tx.t: In this lecture we will look at the diversity of languages around the world. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today.
About forty per cent of them are endangered, which means they are at risk of disappearing. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, while English is the most widely spoken language overall.
Just twenty-three languages account for more than half of the world's population. A language usually disappears when children stop learning it at home.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Kingsley. It began in twenty eleven with one hundred and fifty-six bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by fifty-eight per cent, and on a busy day there were more than seven thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: empty stations at rush hour. The council solved it with a mobile app that shows where bikes are available.
Today, a ride costs one pounds sixty-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: In today's lecture, I will talk about the growth of cities. In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's people lived in cities.
The United Nations expects the figure to reach about two thirds by twenty fifty. Cities take up only about two per cent of the Earth's land, but they produce most of the world's wealth.
Rapid growth can cause housing shortages, traffic jams and air pollution. Some cities are planting trees and building cycle lanes to make urban life healthier.

tx.t: Researchers at Easthaven University carried out a study in twenty twenty-four to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed one hundred and forty-two students over twelve weeks.
On average, the students studied for six hours a day. However, only seventy-four per cent of them used any planned method.
The students who used the method of studying at the same time each day felt less stressed before the exam. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.
